title: Business and Technical Evaluation Checklist
readerIntent: Evaluate whether Nodics fits a proposed product and operating model.
priorKnowledge: Know the product goals, expected users, integrations, and deployment constraints.
summary: Use this checklist to turn a product evaluation into verifiable business, architecture, security, operations, and adoption decisions.

sections.heading: How to use this checklist
paragraphs: Use the checklist during discovery, proof of concept, architecture review, security review, and production readiness. Record an owner, evidence link, decision, risk, and follow-up for every applicable question.

Answers such as supported or not supported are insufficient. Distinguish implemented out-of-the-box behavior, configuration, supported extension, project development, optional provider work, and planned behavior.

sections.heading: Business fit
items: Which reusable Nodics capabilities replace custom foundation work?
Which requirements are project-specific and belong in customer modules?
Which claimed business solutions are already implemented?
What skills and operating responsibilities remain with the adopting organization?

sections.heading: Users and experience
items: Which personas use the solution: customers, employees, administrators, operators, partners, developers, or automated systems?
Which experiences are supplied and which separate frontend applications must the project build?
Can labels, guidance, page composition, localization, and tenant-specific content be changed through governed backend content or configuration?
Are accessibility, responsive layout, mobile webview, localization, time zone, currency, and browser requirements defined?
Can business users complete representative workflows without learning technical module names?

sections.heading: Capability and maturity fit
items: Is each required capability implemented, optional, experimental, project-specific, or only planned?
Which prebuilt providers are available and what maturity evidence exists for each one?
Which business rules are configurable and which require code?
Do technical references identify APIs, schemas, services, configuration, events, jobs, errors, and extension points?
Are limitations and unsupported scenarios explicit?

sections.heading: Architecture and extension
items: Can each requirement be assigned to one authoritative capability?
Can customization use layering or a provider without modifying framework source?
Are tenant, enterprise, server, and node boundaries explicit?
Are APIs and data contracts sufficient for separate frontend applications?

sections.heading: Data and integration
items: Which capability owns each data model and which systems remain external authorities?
How are relationships across models and modules created, validated, searched, imported, exported, and deleted?
What are the tenant, enterprise, catalog, site, store, country, channel, locale, and ownership scopes?
Which database, cache, search, messaging, storage, and AI providers are required?
How are schema evolution, migration, reconciliation, data quality, retention, and archival handled?
Which API, event, file, workflow, and scheduled integrations require idempotency, retry, ordering, or compensation?

sections.heading: Performance and scale
items: What are the expected request rate, concurrency, dataset size, index size, job volume, event volume, and growth assumptions?
Which operations have response-time or completion-time objectives?
Can hot reads use cache or search without creating a second source of truth?
How will modules be grouped into processes, scaled independently, and protected from resource exhaustion?
What load, soak, failover, restart, cache-provider, search-provider, and degraded-dependency tests are required?

sections.heading: Security and operations
items: Are human, service, and scheduled access paths separated?
Are authorization, tenant isolation, audit, rollback, and secret ownership documented?
Are health, logging, metrics, recovery, backup, and scaling responsibilities understood?
Do positive, rejected, boundary, integration, and regression tests provide evidence?

sections.heading: Delivery and customization
items: Can the team explain where framework code ends and customer-project code begins?
Will the project reuse, configure, or extend an existing implementation before adding a new one?
Are generated artifacts rebuilt from source definitions instead of edited manually?
Can two customer projects customize the same capability independently?
Are coding principles, documentation updates, ownership tests, and review gates part of delivery?

sections.heading: Adoption and support
items: Who will train developers, business users, operators, security reviewers, and support teams?
Is beginner-to-expert documentation available for every adopted capability?
Who owns framework upgrades, project compatibility, provider upgrades, incidents, and production support?
What licensing, third-party, cloud, model-token, infrastructure, and partner costs apply?
What pilot success criteria, exit criteria, timeline, and decision authority are agreed?

sections.heading: Required proof before approval
items: A representative end-to-end business scenario demonstrated against current source and configuration.
Successful, rejected, boundary, tenant-isolation, contract, integration, recovery, performance, and regression evidence.
A documented customization performed in a project layer without modifying reusable framework authority.
A deployment and operating model covering topology, secrets, monitoring, backup, restore, scaling, rollback, and incident response.
A gap register separating configuration, extension, new development, provider work, and unsupported requirements.
An accountable adoption plan with cost, skills, ownership, risks, and measurable outcomes.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Business And Technical Evaluation Checklist
paragraphs: Use this checklist before selecting Nodics for a product or customer program. Record evidence, owners, risks, and follow-up actions rather than answering only yes or no.
